title: Mary and Protestants
hook: Protestants honor Mary in their own ways; Luther wrote a commentary on the Magnificat

segments.voice: Yesterday, the May crowning: a child, a statue, a ring of flowers that wilts by the end of the week. Your line was queen of the may. What small thing did you give? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-four.

"My soul doth magnify the Lord." Late in the afternoon, in an old English cathedral, a choir in white robes stands to sing those words. It's Evensong, the evening prayer of the Church of England, and the words are Mary's. On the same evening, in a Catholic monastery, monks sing the same song at Vespers, in Latin, beginning Magnificat. Two buildings, two churches, the same young woman's song rising at dusk. People sometimes assume Mary belongs only to Catholics and the Orthodox, and that Protestants leave her out. The evening tells a more interesting story. Today is about Mary in the churches of the Reformation.
screen: `MY SOUL DOTH MAGNIFY THE LORD.` → `EVENSONG AND VESPERS, AT DUSK.` → `THE SAME SONG IN TWO CHURCHES.`

segments.voice: First, the song itself. In Luke's Gospel, Mary visits her cousin Elizabeth, and answers her greeting with a song. In the Douay-Rheims she says: "for behold from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed." That line is in Luke, and Luke is in Catholic and Protestant Bibles alike. Calling Mary blessed is, quite literally, scripture. Second, Martin Luther. The same reformer who broke with Rome wrote a whole commentary on the Magnificat. He held it up as a lesson in how God looks on the lowly: Mary, a girl of no standing, chosen and lifted up, and the proud scattered. In it, Luther calls her the Mother of God. Third, the prayer book. The Church of England's Book of Common Prayer sets the Magnificat in Evening Prayer, so Anglicans sing Mary's song at dusk, in the prayer book's words: "My soul doth magnify the Lord : and my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour." Fourth, the honest differences. Catholics and Orthodox Christians ask Mary to pray for them, and Catholics hold teachings about her, like the Immaculate Conception, that Protestant churches don't share. Protestant churches also differ among themselves: some keep feasts of Mary on their calendars; some honor her as a model of faith and listening, and pray to God without asking for her prayers. The Second Vatican Council spoke with joy of other Christians who honor the Mother of the Lord. So Mary isn't only a fence line. She's a place where people who disagree about a great deal still stand and sing the same words.
screen: `ALL GENERATIONS SHALL CALL ME BLESSED.` · `LUTHER WROTE ON HER SONG.` · `EVENSONG: MARY'S SONG AT DUSK.` · `WHERE CHURCHES DIFFER, AND WHERE THEY MEET.` · then, large: `MY SOUL DOTH MAGNIFY THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray the Magnificat, or just its first lines. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, you can say slowly, the way choirs do at dusk: "My soul doth magnify the Lord." Breathe. "And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour." Let the words come again, as slowly as you like. If you don't pray, simply hold the picture: two churches across a city, and the same song going up from both at evening. Let the people in them be neighbors for a minute. The bell holds the time.
Mary and Protestants. Churches that differ about Mary, still singing her song: Luther's commentary, the prayer book's Evensong, the Magnificat in Catholic and Protestant Bibles alike. Today's word.
Your line: she belongs to all. Today, look for one thing you share with a Christian from another church: a song, a verse, a prayer you both know. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Catholics sing or say the Magnificat at Vespers, the Church's evening prayer; Anglicans sing it at Evening Prayer (Evensong) from the Book of Common Prayer, and Lutherans also use it at evening services.

notes: The index hook says 'many Protestants honor Mary'; per the claims rule the script hook field drops 'many', and the voice speaks of 'Protestant churches' differing among themselves. The index hook is unchanged.
Luther's commentary is paraphrased ('a lesson in how God looks on the lowly'); Luther's continued use of 'Mother of God' is stated plainly. Confirm both.
'Anglicans have sung Mary's song at dusk for generations' and 'Luke is in every Christian Bible': confirm acceptable without a cited count or date.

The description of Protestant practice ('some keep feasts of Mary... generally pray to God alone rather than asking her prayers') is a generalization; confirm it is fair to Lutherans, Anglicans and other Protestants, and that it ranks no one.
Lumen Gentium 69 paraphrased ('spoke with joy of other Christians who honor the Mother of the Lord'). Confirm.
Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 1:46–48 and the Book of Common Prayer 1662 wording of the Magnificat (with its pointing colon).
howItsDone mentions Lutheran evening services; confirm phrasing.
